03_marg491: It is “confusion,” because there the division of tongues was made.
03_interl604: according to the Hebrews; although Ninus, son of Belus, built it and called it Ninive
03_marg492: The empire of the Assyrians, which was the first, under Ninus, who built Ninive, which because of its penance is called beautiful.
03_interl606: These are the Libyans, who before were Phut
03_marg493: And Mesraim, etc. JEROME. Except for the Laabim, from whom the Libyans were afterwards named, who before were called Phutaeans, and the Casluim, who were afterwards called the Philistim, whom we corruptly call Palestinians, the other six nations are unknown to us, because they were overthrown in the Ethiopian war. And they possessed the land from Gaza to the furthest borders of Egypt.
03_marg494: These names are unknown, either because the nations were destroyed in the Ethiopian war, or because it is not known what names they now have.
03_interl608: from whom Sidon, a city of Phoenicia
03_interl609: these peoples Israel drove out of the land of promise
03_interl610: JEROME. He founded Arca, a town over against Tripolis at the foot of Libanus
03_interl611: who built a city near the one just named, called Sin
03_interl612: from whom the Aradians, who held the island of Aradus
03_interl614: by the Syrians or the Hebrews, Antioch, as among the ancients it is called Emath
03_interl615: these cities are known for their overthrow
03_marg495: He speaks of him last because he follows out his generation and the line of his generation.
03_marg496: Who is yet the fifth from Noe’s son Sem. Whether the Hebrews are said to be named from him, or because through him the generation passes to Abraham? So it is rightly asked which is more likely: that the Hebrews are so called as being Heberites, or as being Abrahamites.
03_interl617: from whom the Elamites, namely the princes of Persia
03_interl621: the Syrians, whose chief city is Damascus
03_interl622: from whom the land of Hus, which the Seventy call Ausitis, that is, the southern; whence “there was a man in the land of Hus whose name was Job.” He founded Trachonitis and Damascus
03_interl623: from whom the Armenians; they hold the part of Asia from the river Euphrates to the Indian Ocean
03_interl624: from whom the Acarnanians, or Carians
03_interl625: from whom are the Maeonians, whom the Seventy call Mosoch, that is, Maeonians
03_interl627: perhaps in his days the division of tongues was made, by which the nations too were divided
03_marg498: And to Heber were born, etc. Heber is “one who passes over,” from whom the Hebrews, that is, those who pass over. They are true Hebrews who pass over from things present to things to come, from things that fall to things that endure.
03_marg499: These nations possessed all the region from the river Cophen which is called Seria.
03_marg500: AUGUSTINE. It was said above that the sons of Noe, or of his sons, were distributed through the lands according to their tongues. But here by way of summing-up he recalls afterwards what was before. But it causes obscurity that he weaves it together in such a manner of speaking as if a telling of things that were done afterwards followed.
03_marg501: They feared a flood again; therefore, with Nemrod as author, they wished to build themselves a tower in which they should not fear a flood.
03_marg502: A foolish and wicked boldness; whence followed vengeance and the division of tongues.
03_marg503: When he fits himself to human senses or works. Whence: “I have seen the affliction of my people, and I am come down to deliver them.” And elsewhere: “I will go down and see whether they have done according to the cry.”
03_marg504: Mystically. The tower is the pride of the world, or the teachings of heretics, who, moved from the east, that is, from the true light, and coming into Sennaar (which is “the shaking out of teeth”), raise up the pride of their teaching against God, wishing by unlawful curiosity to pierce the height of heaven; but, cut off from the unity of faith and the confession of faith, are they not separated from one another by the diversity of error, as by the discord of tongue? A ruinous agreement arms them against God; a sudden confusion of error divides them. The Trinity, against which they have offended, condemns and scatters them. Whence: “Come ye, therefore, let us go down, and there confound their tongue,” namely by the variety of errors or schisms, when the division of tongues was made. In the house of Heber alone the first tongue remained, as in the Church alone, which is the house of Christ, the unity of confession and faith.
03_interl628: the Trinity in persons, as there: “Let us make man,” etc.
03_marg505: He is understood to have said it to the angels. Or according to that: “Let us make man to our image and likeness.” For in the singular number there is added, “and he scattered them,” etc., as there: “God made man to his image and likeness.”
03_marg506: In the Morals, book 2. “Come ye,” etc., is said to those who cleave to God. “Come,” because never to decrease from divine contemplation but always to increase, and never to draw back in heart, is by a steady motion always to come. The angels go up by beholding the Creator; they come down by pressing down, with the scrutiny of strictness, the creature that raises itself unlawfully. So to say, “Let us go down and confound their tongue,” is to show in himself what is rightly done, and by the force of inner vision to breathe into their minds, by hidden movements, the judgments to be shown.
03_interl631: the unity of the Godhead, as there: “God made man to his image,” etc.
03_marg507: ALCUIN. In this division of tongues God made nothing new, but divided the manners of speaking and the forms of speech among the different nations. Whence we find the same syllables and letters of the same value joined otherwise in different tongues, and often the same nouns or verbs signifying something else. Where we say in the psalm, “with a rod of iron,” the Greek has en rhabdō sidēra; but sidera in Latin signifies not “of iron,” as in Greek, but stars.
03_marg508: BEDE. A great question arises for us according to the letter: how Sem is said to be a hundred years old two years after the flood, when above he is asserted to have been born in Noe’s five hundredth year, and the flood is read to have come in the six hundredth year of the same Noe? So that the number of the times may not fight against itself, it is to be understood either that Noe was two years more than five hundred when Sem was born, or two years less than six hundred when the flood came, or that Sem was a hundred and two years old when Arphaxad was born. For Scripture is sometimes wont so to speak that, even if a little is over or short, it gives a full and complete number in the reckoning. But it seems likely, as my guess goes, that when Sem was born Noe was two years over five hundred. Nor did Scripture speak falsely in saying that he was five hundred years old, even if he was five hundred and two, since of course the smaller number is contained within the greater. But perhaps the writer of the holy history took care to set it out more carefully in this place, saying that Sem was a hundred years old two years after the flood, because he remembered that he had noted the year of his birth somewhat loosely.
03_marg509: Nowhere in this whole series of generations has he added “he died,” as in the age that went before the flood; because there was no one in all this line of those born of whom, as an exception from the others, it could be said, as there of Henoch: “And he walked with the Lord, and was seen no more: because God took him.”
03_marg510: JEROME. “These are the generations of Thare,” and the rest. For what we read according to the Seventy, “in the region of the Chaldeans,” the Hebrew has “in Ur Casdim,” that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” And from this occasion the Hebrews hand down a story of this kind: that Abraham was thrown into the fire because he would not worship the fire which the Chaldeans worship, and, freed by God’s help, fled from the fire of idolatry. Where it is written in what follows that Thare went out with his offspring “from the region of the Chaldeans,” in the Hebrew there is “from the burning of the Chaldeans”; and this is what is now said: “And Aran died before Thare his father, in the land of his nativity, in the fire of the Chaldeans,” namely that, not wishing to worship the fire, he was consumed by fire. Afterwards the Lord says to Abram: “I am he who brought thee out of the fire of the Chaldeans.”
03_marg511: AUGUSTINE. Not at once, but at their own times, from when he began to beget. Nor is the order of birth to be heeded here, but the signifying of the dignity to come, in which Abram excels.
03_interl632: consumed by the fire, as the Hebrews say, which he would not worship
03_marg512: In Ur of the Chaldees. In the Hebrew, “in Ur Casdim,” that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” Here the Hebrews tell the story that Abram was thrown into the fire because he would not worship the fire which the Chaldeans worship, and, freed by God’s help, escaped from the fire of idolatry. Whence it is said to him: “I am he who brought thee out from Ur of the Chaldees.”
03_marg513: JEROME. The same Aran, son of Thare, brother of Abraham and Nachor, was father of both: he begot two daughters, Melcha and Sarai, surnamed Jescha. Nachor married Melcha and Abram Sarai; for marriages between uncles and nieces had not yet been forbidden, which in the beginning were held even between brothers and sisters.
03_marg514: And Thare took Abram his son, etc. AUGUSTINE. “And the days of Thare were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran.” It is said first that when Thare was seventy years old he begot Abram, and afterwards he stayed with all his household in Charran and died. And it was said to Abram that he should go out of Charran, and he went out when he was seventy-five years old. But by summing-up it is shown that the Lord commanded it while the father was alive, and that Abram went out of Charran when he was seventy-five years old and his father a hundred and forty-five, if the days of his life were two hundred and five years; so that it is therefore written, “the years of the life of Thare were two hundred and five years in Charran,” because there he filled up the years of his whole life. So the question is solved by summing-up, which is unsolvable if we should say that the Lord told Abram to go out of the land after Thare’s death; because he was not seventy-five years old when his father was already dead, who begot him in the seventieth year of his age, so that after his father’s death he would be a hundred and thirty-five years old, if all the father’s years were two hundred and five. But because some wish Abram’s years to be counted from when he was freed from the fire of the Chaldeans, according to the tradition of the Hebrews, it can be said that the Scripture which says, “When Thare was seventy years old he begot Abram, and Nachor, and Aran,” did not mean that he begot the three in the seventieth year, but recalled when he began to beget. It may be that he begot Abram later, but he was named first by the privilege of dignity, as was done there: “I have loved Jacob, but have hated Esau”; and in Paralipomenon, Juda, fourth in order, was named first, from whom the Jews were named, because of the royal tribe.

03_marg515: Go forth out of thy country, etc. AUGUSTINE. The account of Stephen on this matter is to be considered, so that it may not be contradicted by any of these explanations. And indeed it happened that God did not speak to Abram, as it seems to be told in Genesis, after the death of Thare, that he should go out of his country and from his kindred; but when he was in Mesopotamia, before he dwelt in Charran, having already gone out of the land of the Chaldeans, so that God is understood to have spoken to him on that journey. But because Stephen afterwards tells it thus, “Then Abraham went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan; and from thence, after his father was dead, he removed him into this land,” he brings no small difficulties to this explanation, which is made by summing-up. For he seems to have had the command of the Lord, who had spoken to him on the journey in Mesopotamia when he had gone out of the land of the Chaldeans and was going to Haran, and to have fulfilled it after the death of his father, when it is said, “He dwelt in Charan; and from thence, after his father was dead, he removed him into this land.” And by this the question remains, if he was seventy-five years old when he went out of Charran, how can this be true? Unless perhaps what Stephen says, “Then Abraham went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan,” is taken thus: “then he went out” after the Lord had spoken; for he was already in Mesopotamia (as was said above) when he heard it from the Lord. But by the rule of summing-up Stephen wished to weave it together and say at once from where he went out and where he dwelt, when he says: “Then Abram went out of the land of the Chaldeans and dwelt in Charan.” But in between, that is, between the going out of the land of the Chaldeans and the dwelling in Charran, God spoke to him. And as to what Stephen adds, “and from thence, after his father was dead, God removed him into this land,” it is to be noted that he does not say, “and after his father was dead he went out of Charran,” but, “from thence God removed him into this land”; so that after the dwelling in Charran he was settled in the land of Chanaan: not that he went out after his father’s death, but that he was settled in the land of Chanaan. So that the order of the words is: he dwelt in Charran, and from thence he removed him into this land after his father was dead; namely, he was settled then when he received there the grandson whose whole seed was to reign, by God’s promise, the inheritance being given. For from Abraham himself was born Ismael of Agar, and others of Cetura, and of Isaac Esau, to whom the inheritance does not belong; but of Jacob, the son of Isaac, as many as were born, that is, his whole seed, belonged to that inheritance. So Abram was settled in that land in this way, when he lived there until the birth of Jacob.
03_marg516: It is to be noted that he had already gone out of his country; but then he had gone out in body, not in mind and will, for he perhaps had a mind to return when it was said to him: “Go forth,” etc.
03_marg517: He left the land, the time, the kindred of the Jews, and was magnified among the peoples of the Gentiles. Two things are promised to Abram: namely, that his seed shall possess the land of Chanaan, when it is said, “and come into the land which I shall shew thee”; but the other, far more excellent, is not of the fleshly but of the spiritual seed, by which he is to be the father not only of the Jewish nation but of all nations that follow his faith; which is promised thus: “And in thee shall all the kindred of the earth be blessed.”

03_marg519: JEROME. If Thare, Abraham’s father, begot Abram in the region of Chaldea at seventy years old, and died in Charran in his two hundred and fifth year, how is Abram recorded as going out of Charran after Thare’s death at seventy-five years old, when from his birth to his father’s death there are shown to have been a hundred and thirty-five years? So the tradition of the Hebrews is true, that Thare went out with his sons from the fire of the Chaldeans, and that Abram, hemmed in by the Babylonian fire because he would not worship it, was freed by God’s help, and that from that time the span of his age is reckoned to him, from when he confessed God, spurning the idols of the Chaldeans. But it may be, since Scripture has left it uncertain, that Thare, having set out from Chaldea, came into Haran a few years before he died, or straight after the persecution, and stayed there a long time.

03_marg522: Say, therefore, I pray thee, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked why the patriarch wished to lie so as to call her his sister, and did not rather commit it to God, who, if he wished, could keep her chastity safe with Pharao. But he wished the truth to be hidden, yet not a lie to be told. For she is called a sister because she was a brother’s daughter. And in this it is shown that no one should tempt his God while he has something he can do by reasonable counsel. For he did for his life what he could; but what he could not, he committed to God, in whom he hoped, to whom he entrusted his wife’s chastity; nor did faith or hope deceive him. So let a man not dare to tempt God while he has a reasonable way to escape what he ought to beware of. Nor did Paul despair of God’s protection or lose faith when, let down in a basket, he escaped the hands of his enemies. But Abram himself, if when asked he had declared her his wife, would have committed two things to God: both his own life and his wife’s chastity.
03_marg523: RABANUS. Sarai is excused, who is taken into the house of Pharao against her will, not only in this, that the body is not defiled, nor the soul, except by the mind’s consent, but also in this, that it was done with her husband’s agreement and permission.
03_marg524: She could remain untouched so long with Pharao because it is read in Esther that the maidens were not brought in to the kings at once, but were kept for a year, and for six months were anointed with oil of myrrh, and for another six months were in various perfumes. So through this respite of time she could remain untouched, and meanwhile the Egyptians used Abram well, until Pharao, scourged by God and learning that she was his wife, gave her back untouched.

03_marg525: And Abram went up, etc. JEROME. Freed from Egypt, he is well read to have gone up. But how could he be very rich? But in the Hebrew truth there is “exceedingly heavy,” for he was weighed down by the weight of Egypt. And though they seem to be riches of gold and silver, yet if they are Egyptian they are heavy to a holy man. Nor is it, as is read in the Seventy, “he went whence he had come, into the desert, as far as Bethel,” but according to the Hebrew, “he went on his journey through the south as far as Bethel.” For he set out from Egypt not to make for the desert, which he had left in Egypt, but to come through the south, which is opposite the north, to the house of God, where his tent was, between Bethel and Hai.

03_marg526: To Bethel, etc. Bethel is a small town at the twelfth milestone from Aelia, on the right as one goes to Neapolis, which was before called Luza, that is, almond tree, in the tribe of Benjamin. But Hai is in the tribe of Juda, set apart for the priests. Bethel is “house of God”; Hai, “eye” or “fountain.” So, pitching his tent between Bethel and Hai, he rightly built an altar to the Lord, because the saints, withdrawing from the prince of the world and the pleasures of the age, washed in the holy fountain of baptism, leading the course of the present life with care, and offering to God the sacrifice of praise and of good work upon the altar of faith, happily make for the house of God, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.

03_marg527: Let there be no quarrel, I beseech thee, etc. Let us too put nothing before concord and charity, but through the right hand of prosperity or the left of adversity persevere in peace and love. The strife between Lot’s herdsmen and Abraham’s herdsmen signifies the controversy between catholic pastors and heretical subverters. Whence Lot, who is interpreted “turning aside,” signifies the heresiarchs, and he chose for himself the region about the Jordan, that is, “descent.” His herdsmen signify heretics and schismatics, who seek what is fair and sloping, and do not go up the mountain with Moses to the Lord; despising peace and unity, they take the choice of going where they will, and fleeing grace they commit themselves to free will. But Abraham’s herdsmen signify catholic teachers, who flee heretics even in place, according to that: “A man that is a heretic, after the first and second admonition, avoid.” And this in the land of the Chanaanite and the Pherezite, namely in the land of promise; because between catholics and heretics there is wont to be contention over whose is the kingdom of heaven.

03_marg537: JEROME. In Hebrew it is called “devouring.” The Hebrews hand down that elsewhere it is called Salissa and “the heifer of three years,” because it was swallowed up by a third earthquake. After Sodom and Gomorrha, Adama and Seboim were overthrown by divine fire, it is called “the little one”; for Segor is rendered “little,” which in the Syrian tongue is called Zoara. But the vale of the salt pits, in which there were pits of bitumen, after God’s anger and the rain of sulphur, was turned into the Dead Sea, which is called by the Greeks the lake of asphalt, that is, of bitumen.

03_marg539: Such kings overcome first Bara, who is interpreted “malice” or “creature,” and is king of Sodom, that is, of blindness or of the silent beast, when they persuade those who persist in their old malice to follow the blindness of lust after the manner of beasts. They overcome also Bersa, that is, one set in straits, king of Gomorrha, that is, of a swelling and seditious people, when they overwhelm and lay low those who are straitened by the cares of the world and do not fear to commit the wickedness of robbery. They overcome also Sennaab, king of Adama, that is, of the earthly, when they urge those who savour only earthly things to remain in luxury, so that they say: “Let us eat and drink, for to morrow we shall die.” They overcome Semeber, who is interpreted “there perdition,” and is king of Seboim, that is, of the girdle of mourning, when through anger and envy they deceive the unwary. Whence: “Anger killeth the foolish, and envy slayeth the little one.” They overcome the king of Bala too, when they send the faint-hearted into despair. For Bala is interpreted “casting headlong” or “swallowing up”: the devil strives most of all for this, that after the fall of sin he may send a man into despair.

03_marg544: ISIDORE. In like manner our faith, when it has been strengthened by the principal spirit, subdues the five senses of the body as five kings, triumphing over the outward man by the word of God. He overcame his enemies with three hundred and eighteen, because we, in the sacrament of the cross, which the letter tau signifies, which stands for three hundred, overcome the five fleshly senses that before took us captive by various vices. Eighteen, multiplied from three and six, signifies faith in the Trinity and the perfection of work, by which the full victory of the virtues against the vices is accomplished.
03_marg545: Allegorically. Abraham’s war with the four kings signifies the war of virtues and vices. For the letter tau, which has the shape of a cross, expresses three hundred.

03_marg547: But Melchisedech, etc. JEROME. The Hebrews say that this is Sem, the son of Noe, and show by the reckoning of years that he lived until Isaac, and that all the firstborn from Noe to Aaron were high priests. And Salem was afterwards called Jerusalem. The apostle, recalling Melchisedech “without father, without mother,” refers him to Christ, and through him to the Church of the Gentiles, because the glory of the head is referred to the members. Since he blessed Abram the circumcised, and in him Levi, and so Aaron too, from whom the priesthood came afterwards; from which he wishes to gather that the priesthood of the Church, which has the foreskin, blessed the circumcised priesthood of the synagogue. And what he says, “Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech,” our ministry is marked by the word “order”: to be consecrated not through Aaron by sacrificing irrational victims, but by bread and wine being offered, that is, the body and blood of the Lord.

So the patriarch, knowing that the priesthood among the people of the Gentiles was better than the Levitical, which was to be born of himself, and that he was to be blessed by the better, gave Melchisedech the tithes of his substance after the blessing, as the people according to the laws gave tithes to the priests who blessed them. Melchisedech is interpreted “king of peace” or “of justice.” For we are reconciled to God through Christ, who is to come to sort the good from the evil. He is the priest who offered himself to God the Father for all, and the true king, who rules his own in the present and in the future will judge justly.

03_marg550: From the very woof thread, etc. The just man shakes his hands from every gift; in which it is shown that wars are to be waged by the faithful not out of greed but out of charity. He excepts the pay of the soldiers and the shares of those who had fought together with him, partly showing his own justice, partly not denying the pay owed to those who fight lawfully.

Their wavering is removed by the prophetic spirit, and their faith, made firm, earns justice. Whence: “Abram believed God, and it was reputed to him unto justice.”

03_marg555: RABANUS. A twofold signifying of the promised seed is given. When the stars are shown, it is said to him, “So will I make thy seed,” that is, the Christian nation, of which thou art to be father in faith, namely to shine with the light of the resurrection. But when the sand is shown it is said, “So shall thy seed be,” etc., that is, the nation of the Jews will be numerous, but dry and barren.

03_marg556: Take me, he said, a cow, etc. ISIDORE. The three-year-old cow is the people set under the yoke of the law; the she goat, the same people that was to be a sinner; the ram signifies it as about to reign. These are called three years old because through the joints of the times, from Adam to Noe, and from there to Abram, and from there to David, the nation grew up as to a three-year age. By the turtle and the pigeon the spiritual peoples are figured, the sons of the promise and heirs of the kingdom to come, whose age is not told, who, meditating on eternal things, pass beyond the temporal. The three-year-old animals are divided, the parts being set against each other, because the fleshly, both in the old people and now, are separated from one another. The birds are not divided, because the spiritual are led astray neither by schism nor by heresy, but enjoy peace, whether they live alone like the turtle or with others like the pigeon. The fowls coming down upon the divided bodies signify demons seeking food for themselves from the division of the fleshly. Abram driving away the birds signifies that many fleshly men are to be freed at the end of the world through the merit of the saints. About the setting of the sun fear fell upon Abram, and a great and darksome horror seized him, because about the end of the age a great disturbance from Antichrist will seize the saints. Whence: “There shall be tribulation such as hath not been from the beginning.” So, “when the sun was set,” etc., signifies the day of judgment to come after the end of the age, when through fire the good will be separated from the evil.
03_marg557: Because from Adam to Noe, and from there to Abram, and then to David, the people grew up.

03_marg558: And the fowls came down, etc. GREGORY. Tropologically. In the very sacrifice of prayer troublesome thoughts thrust themselves in, wishing to snatch or defile it; but with the hand of holy discernment we must guard what we offer outwardly, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts snatch it away.
03_interl787: because about the end of the world a great disturbance will be brought upon the saints by Antichrist
03_marg559: Fear fell upon, etc. AUGUSTINE. This question is to be treated because of those who contend that such disturbances do not fall upon the mind of the wise man. Whether it is such as Gellius recalls: namely that a certain philosopher was disturbed in a great storm at sea, and was noticed by a certain dissolute young man, who, after the danger, mocked him because the philosopher had been so quickly disturbed. He answered that the young man had not been disturbed because he had no need to fear anything for his most worthless soul, since it was not worth fearing anything for. But to the others he brought out a book, in which it was read that the Stoics did not hold that no such disturbance falls upon the mind of the wise man, as if nothing of the kind appeared in their feelings; but that disturbance was defined by them as when reason gave way to such movements; and when it did not give way, it was not to be called a disturbance.
03_interl790: Isidore: in affliction the three hundred years will be completed
03_interl791: in the last part of this time
03_marg560: Know thou beforehand, etc. ISIDORE. The people of Israel is prophesied as to serve in Egypt; not that it served the Egyptians for four hundred years, but because this number was completed in that affliction, since it is counted from the time when these things were promised to Abram.
03_marg561: Know thou beforehand, etc. It is not to be taken as if the people of God were four hundred years in that most hard slavery. But because it was said, “In Isaac shall thy seed be called,” from the beginning of Isaac’s birth to the year of Israel’s going out of Egypt four hundred and five years are counted. So when you have taken from four hundred and thirty the twenty-five which run from the promise to the birth of Isaac, it is no wonder if Scripture wished to call the four hundred and five years by a round sum; for it is wont so to number times that what goes a little over the sum of a number, or is under it, is not counted. So what he says, “they shall bring them under bondage and afflict them,” is not to be referred to the three hundred years, as if for so many years they held them in bondage; but the years are to be referred to what was said, “thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own.” For whether in the land of Chanaan or in Egypt, it was a stranger until it should have the inheritance by God’s promise, which happened after they were freed from Egypt. So that by hyperbaton the order of the words is: “Know thou certainly that thy seed shall be a stranger in a land not their own four hundred years”; and “they shall bring them under bondage and afflict them” is put in between, so that this insertion does not belong to the four hundred years. For in the last part of this sum, that is, after the death of Joseph, the people of God was afflicted in Egypt with hard slavery.

03_marg562: But in the fourth generation, etc. JEROME. But Moses says elsewhere, “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up out of the land of Egypt”; yet they went out in the fourth generation. For Levi begot Caath, Caath begot Amram, he Aaron, Aaron Eleazar, and he begot Phinees. Caath went into Egypt with his father Levi; Eleazar went out with Aaron. From Caath to Eleazar, four generations. Some, however, begin from Amram and come to Phinees. But they went out in the fifth generation because Juda begot Phares, Phares begot Esron, Esron begot Aram, Aram begot Aminadab, Aminadab begot Naasson, who begot Salmon. Phares went into Egypt with his father Juda; Naasson is entered as prince of the tribe of Juda in the desert, whose son Salmon entered the land of promise. From Phares to Naasson, five generations. Some, however, begin from Esron and come to Salmon.

03_marg563: Now Sarai the wife, etc. RABANUS. Abram is not an adulterer if he is joined to a handmaid while his wife is living, because the law of the Gospels of one wife had not yet been proclaimed; and he had heard that his race was to be multiplied, but did not know by which woman, for he knew that Sara was barren. Nor was there lustful pleasure in the union, but the godly love of having offspring. His wife too wished it and pressed it, who could not have sons; therefore she desired to receive from another one whom she might adopt in the place of her own.
03_interl804: room is given to fleshly observance, because the time of grace had not yet come
03_marg564: Go in unto my handmaid, etc. JEROME. Note carefully that the getting of sons is called in Hebrew “building.” For there it is read: “Go in unto my handmaid, if perhaps I may be built up from her.” This is what is said in Exodus: “And God blessed the midwives, and they built themselves houses.”
03_marg565: Agar signifies the earthly Jerusalem, in which the old law was practised in a fleshly and servile way; but Sara the grace of the New Testament, which bears free children, citizens of the Jerusalem above. But the grace of the New Testament was long not in the open, and gave the Old Testament, as a handmaid, leave to beget: servants, namely, serving from fear, not love, as if begetting sons of Abraham’s seed, whom it should bind to the worship of the one God and call back from idols, to which the Gentiles offered like sacrifices. But when that people, puffed up by the works of the flesh, refused grace at Christ’s coming and remained unbelieving in slavery, grace prevailing, it was so afflicted and saddened that it lost kingdom and priesthood. Whence, brought into the wilderness, thirsting for the fountain of the law by diligent searching and meditating, it finds nothing, except that, at the warning of the law given through Moses as through an angel, it should return to grace and submit itself.
03_marg566: Mystically. These two women are the two Testaments: Agar the Old, which in the synagogue nourished the Jewish people, bound to slavery; Sara the New, which begot the Christian people into the freedom of faith. The handmaid’s sons were multiplied, so that they could not be numbered for multitude, who above are compared to the sand. So this people, jealous in its fierceness and contrary to all good men, above all when, goaded by envy, it persecutes the Christian people through the whole world, is also, scattered far and wide in wandering and trading, burdensome to all.

JEROME: in the Hebrew there is phara, which is interpreted “wild ass.” It signifies that his seed would dwell in the desert, that is, the wandering Saracens, with no fixed seats, who, raiding all the nations whose side borders on the desert, are fought against by all.
03_marg568: She rightly called his name so, because he freely takes counsel for the wretched and comforts the humble. Whence: “Thou considerest labour and sorrow; to thee is the poor man left,” etc. “Verily here have I seen the hinder parts of him that seeth me.” Such is that: “Thou shalt see my back parts: but my face thou canst not see. For man shall not see me and live.” For no one can see that manifestation of the wisdom of God and live. It is that beauty for which he sighs who loves God with his whole heart, his whole soul, his whole mind; to contemplate which he also builds up his neighbour as far as he can, by loving him as himself. But his hinder parts, that is, his incarnation, which he took on in the last times, we now contemplate by desiring through faith and love; in the future we shall enjoy them in eternal contemplation.
03_marg569: Therefore she called that well, etc. To this day the well of Agar is shown in the desert of Arabia between Cades and Barad. It signifies the scripture of the old law and the new, which our Maker, the life of the living, the hope of the dying, gave to mortals in the regard of his loving mercy, so that, taught and corrected from vices, they may deserve to be worthy for ever of the vision of God.

03_marg571: JEROME. The Hebrews say that God added to Abraham and Sara the letter he from his own name, which among them is the four-lettered one. For he was called Abram, which is “high father”; afterwards he was called Abraham, which is “father of many”; for “nations” is not in the name but understood. Nor is it to be wondered at that, while among the Greeks and us the letter a seems to be added, the letter he is said to be added; for the idiom of the Hebrew tongue is wont to write he and read a, as on the contrary to pronounce e and write a.

03_marg573: AUGUSTINE. Scripture calls eternal that whose end is not fixed, or which is not done in such a way that it must not be done afterwards, as far as belongs to the care or power of the doer. Whence: “He will be a slave for ever who will not know how to use a little.”

03_marg574: STRABO. For three reasons this is commanded to Abraham. First, that he might please by obedience to the command, through whose transgression Adam had displeased. Second, that by this sign he might be distinguished from the other nations. Third, that, being circumcised in that member in which lust is wont to rule, he might know that chastity was to be kept by him and unchastity cut away.

03_marg575: RABANUS. STRABO. Circumcision done in one member signifies the spiritual circumcision, which is to be shown in the heart and in all the senses. The heart is to be circumcised, lest we think harmful things; the eyes, lest we see vanity; the ears are to be circumcised, that is, stopped, lest they hear blood. And so in all the senses circumcision is to be kept.
03_marg576: Therefore circumcision was commended to Abraham, that he might be under law; as Adam was, that he should not eat of the tree, so that it might be proved whether this would be fulfilled or not. For Abraham believed that he would have a son in whom all nations should be blessed, and in whose descendants a pattern of chastity and sobriety should remain. Hence he received the sign of faith there whence Isaac was to be born, a son of God, not of the flesh: not more unsightly for the cutting off of a part of the body, but more glorious by the sign of faith. So to lose something for God is gain, not loss. If Adam had kept God’s covenant, Abraham would not have received this covenant. But because Adam first knew the guilt of disobedience in this member, it was fitting that Abraham secondly should receive the sign of obedience in this member; so that thus it might be shown that the obedient would one day beget sons to life whence the transgressors once begot them to death.
03_marg577: Already then, because of the sojourning to come, lest his seed be mingled with the nations, the covenant of circumcision is given as a sign; for it signifies nature renewed through baptism after the stripping off of the old man through Christ, who rose after the sabbath. He commanded the servants too, those born in the house and those bought, to be circumcised, to teach that the grace of redemption belongs to all. There too the parents’ names are changed, so that all things may sound of newness: Abram, “high father”; Abraham, “father of many nations.”

03_marg578: ISIDORE. It is asked how uncircumcised children, who do not make God’s covenant void, but rather those who neglected to circumcise them, should perish. But they made God’s covenant void not by their own work but by their origin, in the first man, in whom all sinned. For all are born sinners not by their own act but by origin. Therefore all perish who are not freed through regeneration.
03_marg579: ISIDORE. The promise of the calling of the nations is made plain in Isaac, the son of the promise, that is, of grace, not of nature, because he came of an old father and a barren mother. And because this was to be not through generation, as with Ismael, but through regeneration, circumcision was commanded when a son of Sara was promised, in the type of the Church, not when Ismael was, who is the type of the Jews.
03_marg580: ISIDORE. They err who think that Sara was first written with one r and that afterwards another r was added, and because r among the Greeks signifies a hundred, they guess many absurdities about this name; when, however they would have the word changed, it must have not a Greek but a Hebrew reason, for it is Hebrew. For no one, naming someone in one tongue, takes the etymology of the word from another. So she was first called Sarai, with shin, resh, yod. So the yod being taken away, the letter he was added, which is read as a, and she was called Sara. For before she was called “my princess,” as the mother of one household; afterwards absolutely “princess,” namely the princess-to-be of all nations. Some very wrongly guess that she was first called “leprosy” and afterwards “princess,” since leprosy is called sarat, which in our tongue seems to have some likeness, but in Hebrew is wholly different; for it is written with tsade and ayin and resh and tau, which plainly differs from the three above, that is, shin, resh and he, with which Sara is written.

03_marg581: Abraham fell upon his face, etc. JEROME. A little later follows: “And thou shalt call his name Isaac,” which is interpreted “laughter,” from Abraham’s laughter, not Sara’s. For it is after his son was called Isaac from Abraham’s laughter that Sara is read to have laughed.

03_marg583: I will establish my covenant with him, etc. The covenant of the Lord is with Isaac, namely the faithful people, which mother Church has begotten through faith and baptism; and an everlasting covenant, because the possession of eternal life is promised to it alone, which with its head Christ shall possess the kingdom of heaven for ever.

03_marg585: The next year, in which Sara bore Isaac, is the times of regeneration, in which the blood of Christ was shed and the human race restored to life.

03_marg586: And Abraham took, etc. God did not intend only that the foreskin of the flesh of Abraham and his offspring should be circumcised, but he was bestowing the gifts of the eternal testament on him whom he had chosen out of all. Whence Paul: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in spirit.” And elsewhere: “For it is not he is a Jew, who is so outwardly; nor is that circumcision which is outwardly in the flesh.” So let us circumcise by the word of God the ears, the lips, the heart, the foreskin and all the members of the flesh. Of the circumcision of the ears it is said: “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.” With uncircumcised ears we cannot hear the words of wisdom and truth. Let us circumcise the lips, lest we speak anything shameful or evil or idle. He circumcises the flesh of the foreskin who uses marriage only for the sake of offspring, at fixed and lawful times; he who acts otherwise does not circumcise. But the Church, strengthened by the grace of Christ crucified for her, not only keeps herself from unlawful things but even from those allowed, and as a virgin bride of Christ flowers in chaste virgins, in whom the true circumcision of the foreskin is kept in the flesh. But he who commits no adultery by obscene desires, or by heretical meanings and blasphemous assertions, but keeps the purity of faith in his conscience, is circumcised in heart, and of him it can be said: “Blessed are the clean of heart,” etc. Let the hands be circumcised, lest they do evil; the feet, lest they run to evil; the sight, lest it covet unlawful things; the taste, that it may eat and drink to the glory of God; the smell, that it may take in the odour of Christ and by works of mercy spread the odour of sweetness. Each member too, if it serves God in its offices, is circumcised; if it runs riot beyond the prescribed law, uncircumcised.
03_marg587: STRABO. It is often asked how women were saved, who were not circumcised. By faith, namely, and the offering of sacrifices, as holy men were cleansed before circumcision. Whence: “purifying their hearts by faith.”

03_marg588: ISIDORE. Abraham bears a threefold figure. The first, of the Saviour, who, leaving his kindred, came into the world. The second, of the Father, because he sacrificed his only son. The third (which appears in this place), of the saints, who received the coming of Christ with joy. Abraham’s tent signifies Jerusalem, where for a time the prophets and apostles dwelt, and where Christ, coming, was received by those who believed and hung on the wood by those who did not.
03_interl896: because to those so disposed faith in the Trinity is made known
03_marg589: Allegorically. The three men announce the coming of Christ, whom two angels accompany: according to some, Moses and Elias. The one is the lawgiver, who in the law pointed to the Lord’s coming; the other, who is to come at the end, will announce the second coming of Christ and preach his gospel. Whence, when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, they are seen with him.
03_marg590: He saw three and adored one, namely showing the Saviour whose coming he was awaiting. Whence: “Abraham saw my day, and was glad.” For he foresaw the mystery of the sacrament to come. Hence he washed their feet, to show the cleansing of the laver that was to come at the end of the world; for the feet signify the last things.
03_interl897: with eagerness for hospitality, leaving us this as an example
03_marg591: GREGORY. Morally. Abraham runs to meet three angels, because the man and lord of the house, namely the spiritual understanding, must by the knowledge of the Trinity go beyond the bars of the flesh, and, as it were, go out of the door of its lowest dwelling. The care of the flesh, which Sara signifies, should not appear outside for display, but behind the man’s back, that is, under the discernment of the spirit, intent only on necessary things, should not know how to uncover itself boldly, but to keep itself modestly in check.
03_marg592: Abraham could not have seen angels, received them as guests and set food before them, unless they had taken bodies from the air. For they would not appear, nor take food, unless they had a solid body from a heavenly element. Nor is it any wonder that they are called now angels, now the Lord; because those are called angels who minister outwardly, and the Lord is shown who commands inwardly.

03_marg593: He turns back to the duties of hospitality, which can be shown even to angels when they take on a bodily form from the elements. Understanding this, Abraham adored the Godhead in unity and ministered to the angelic dispensation in its visible form.
03_interl903: so that I may show you these services

03_marg594: These things are said in the type of the Church, which has been gathered from the three parts of the world into the unity of faith, and, as bread without leaven, baked by the fire of the Spirit.
03_marg595: STRABO. A satum is a kind of measure. The three measures signify the three sons of Noe, from whom the whole race was spread abroad. So the Church is signified, or the gospel teaching, which was to be spread through the whole world and multiplied in the three parts of the world: Asia, Africa and Europe.
03_marg596: Of which Sara makes cakes upon the hearth. These are the three measures of meal which the woman in the Gospel leavened. The loaves are unleavened, because the unity of believers must be without the leaven of malice, the weakness of wickedness, and the heat of perverse teaching.

03_marg605: Now they were both old, etc. The elderly age is younger than that of the old, even if the elderly are called old. Whence, if according to the physicians an elderly man cannot get children of an elderly woman, even if her courses still flow, according to this Abraham wonders at God’s power over the promise of a son; and we can take it that the apostle set down this miracle. For his body was not altogether dead to begetting, if the woman had been of youthful age; but he could not beget of one advanced in age. For afterwards he begot of Cetura, because she was young. For the physicians hold that an old man cannot beget of a woman of more advanced age (even if her courses still come to her), but can of a young one. Again, a woman of advanced age, even if her courses still come to her, cannot bear of an elderly man, but can of a young one. So it was a miracle, because both were old and far advanced in years, and it had ceased to be with Sara after the manner of women.
03_marg606: GREGORY. Morally. When the care of the flesh is often told not to presume upon itself but to put its whole self into trust in the divine hope, it despises it, and, its own effort ceasing, distrusts that the supports of life will be at hand for it. Whence Sara, hearing God’s promises, laughs; but laughing she is rebuked, and rebuked she is at once made fruitful; and she who could not be made fruitful when strong in youth conceived when broken by old age; because when the care of the flesh leaves off having confidence in itself, against hope it receives from the divine promise what it doubted by human reason that it would have. Whence he who is begotten is rightly called “laughter”; for when our mind conceives trust in the hope above, what does it bring forth but joy?

03_marg612: Morally. Wealth does not lift some up through pride, but through works of mercy. Some, when they see themselves abounding in earthly things, do not seek the true riches and do not love the eternal kingdom, because they think temporal things enough. So it is not wealth that is at fault but the disposition; for all things that God made are good. But he who uses good things badly brings it about that, through the gluttony of greed, he dies by the bread by which he should have lived. Poor Lazarus came to rest; torments tortured the proud rich man. Abraham, who held Lazarus in his bosom, had been rich; yet he says: “I will speak to my Lord, whereas I am dust and ashes.” What did he think of his riches, who reckoned himself dust and ashes? We see plainly in what place he had set himself, who reckoned himself dust and ashes even when he spoke with God. With what punishment, then, are they to be struck who do not advance to the highest things and are lifted up over the least?

In Sodom, which was to be destroyed because of its womanish softness, two appear, because two is the first to depart from unity and is the beginning of alternation. Since Lot wished to prostitute his daughters with this compensation, that his just guests should suffer nothing of the kind from the Sodomites, it is rightly asked whether a compensation of crimes, or of any sins whatever, is to be admitted, so that we do some evil lest another do a worse evil; or whether rather it is to be put down to Lot’s disturbance, not to his counsel, that he said this. 03_marg634: There is this city here. That is, Sodom, which is interpreted “blindness,” expresses worldly desires; but the height of the mountains is the contemplation of the perfect. He went out indeed from Sodom, but yet did not reach the mountains; because many just men flee indeed the enticements of the world, but, set in action, cannot climb to the peak of contemplation; with which agrees what the same Lot says: “There is a city near.” So it is called near, and yet is shown safe for salvation; because the active life is neither wholly separated from the cares of the world nor yet a stranger to the joy of eternal salvation. Otherwise: to flee burning Sodom is to turn aside from the unlawful kindlings of the flesh; the height of the mountains is the stronghold of the continent.

But because many flee the enticements of the world, yet, set in action, cannot climb to the peak of contemplation, Lot went out of Sodom but did not reach the mountains. Whence Lot says: “There is this city here at hand,” etc. It is called near, and yet safe for salvation, because the active life is neither wholly separated from the cares of the world nor a stranger to the joy of eternal salvation.
03_marg636: Morally. To flee burning Sodom is to turn aside from the fires of the flesh. The height of the mountains is contempt of the world. Or those are on the mountain who cleave to fleshly union, but are not loosed into any pleasure of the flesh except for the care of receiving offspring. But many forsake the crimes of the flesh, and yet, set in the marriage of the flesh, do not keep only the laws of due use. Lot went out of Sodom but did not at once reach the mountains, because the damnable life is left, but the height of conjugal continence is not yet strictly held. In the middle is Segor, to save the weak fugitive; because when married people come together through incontinence, they flee the falls of crimes and are saved with pardon, and find as it were a little city in which they are defended from the fires; because married life is not wonderful in virtues, but only safe from punishments. Whence: “There is this city here,” etc. Married people guard their life as in a little city when they intercede for themselves with constant prayers. Whence it is said to Lot: “Behold also in this I have heard thy prayers”; because when prayer is poured out to God, such a married life is not condemned. Whence: “Defraud not one another,” etc.

03_marg639: ALCUIN. The infants were burned with their parents in Sodom, so that the most wicked deed of the Sodomites might be noticed, lest any trace of their origin should remain. And it was provided for them, lest, living long, they should follow the examples of their fathers and be punished more lightly. The parents too are guilty, as much for them as for themselves; for the death of the children is the crime of the parents. Therefore they will be their accusers. And it is some kind of benefit not to be guilty, for one who is not glorious; for it profits one not to be poor who cannot be a king.

03_marg640: ISIDORE. Lot’s wife is the figure of the kind of people who, called by grace, look back and strive to return to what they had left; of whom it is said: “No man putting his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.” Therefore they are forbidden to look back. In which it is shown that there is no going back to the old life for those who, regenerated by grace, desire to escape the last fire. The wife, looking back, was turned into salt, made namely an example and a seasoning by which others may be salted. Whence Christ says: “Remember Lot’s wife,” namely that he might season us as with salt, so that we should not be careless but beware prudently.

03_marg645: And Lot went up out of Segor, etc. JEROME. It is asked why, when he first preferred Segor to flight to the mountain and wished the city where he should dwell to be spared, he again passed from Segor to the mountain. We shall answer that the conjecture of the Hebrews about Segor is true: that, often overwhelmed by earthquake, it was first called Bala and afterwards Salisa; and Lot was afraid, saying: “If, while the others stood, this one was often overthrown, how much less will it be able to be saved in the common ruin?” And that this occasion of unbelief was the cause of the incest. For he who had seen the others overthrown and this one stand, and himself rescued by God’s help, ought not to have doubted what he had heard granted to him.
03_marg646: And the elder said to the younger, etc. JEROME. This is said in excuse of the daughters, that they thought the human race had failed, and therefore lay with their father. But what follows does not excuse the father: “and he perceived not when they lay with him, nor when they rose from him.” The Hebrews mark it above with an obelus as superfluous, as if it were incredible, because the nature of things does not allow anyone to have intercourse without knowing it.

03_marg649: Come, let us make him drunk, etc. ALCUIN. Lot’s two daughters had learned that the end of the world was to come by fire. But as girls not fully instructed, they did not know that, the Sodomites being laid waste by fire, much space would remain whole; and they suspected that something had happened such as they had heard of in the times of Noe, and that they were left with their father to restore the human race. And though lying with their father was a great crime, it seemed a heavier impiety if, by keeping chastity, they should blot out the hope of posterity. This appears more in what follows, when it is said: “And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: By my own self have I sworn, saith the Lord.” For it is not easily found that Christ would call the Father “Lord,” as his own Lord, especially before the incarnation. For according to the flesh this is fittingly said, according to which it is said in the psalm, “The Lord said to,” etc. But what is said, “The Lord said to my Lord,” is referred to the prophet who speaks; like that, “The Lord rained from the Lord,” that is, our Lord, namely the Son, from our Lord, namely the Father.

03_marg695: ALCUIN. The ram that was sacrificed for Isaac was not imaginary but real. Therefore the angel is thought rather to have brought it from elsewhere than to have created it there from the earth after the work of the six days.
03_marg696: A ram amongst the briers sticking fast, etc. JEROME. Aquila put “a brier” or “a thorn thicket,” and, as the rendering of the word is, thick shrubs entwined with one another. Whence Symmachus, led by the same opinion, says: “And there appeared after these things a ram held in a net by its horns.” But the Seventy and Theodotion seem to render better, who put the very name sabech: “in the bushes of sabech, by its horns.” For sichon, or “net,” which Aquila and Symmachus put, is written with the letter shin; but here the letter samech is put. Whence it is plain that the word sabech is not a rendering of thick stems and shrubs woven together in the manner of a net, but sounds the name of a bush which is so called in Hebrew.

03_marg697: And he called the name, etc. JEROME. Whence too, as a sign of the ram that was given, they are wont to sound a horn.

03_marg699: JEROME. Of Melcha, wife of Nachor, daughter of Aran, was born Hus, from whose stock Job came down, as it is written: “There was a man in the land of Hus, whose name was Job.” So some think wrongly that Job was of the race of Esau; for what is had at the end of his book, that it was translated from the Syrian tongue, and that he was fourth from Esau, and the rest that is contained there, is not had in the Hebrew. Second was born of Melcha Buz, of whose race was Balaam the soothsayer, as the Hebrews hand down; who in Job is called Eliu: at first a holy man and a prophet of God, afterwards, through disobedience and the desire of gifts, when he wished to curse Israel, he is called by the name of soothsayer. Whence: “And Eliu the son of Barachel the Buzite was angry,” etc. But Camuel is the father of Damascus; for it is called Aram, which here is written for Syria, and by that very name it is read in Isaias.

For Arboch signifies nothing at all; but it is called Arbee, that is, “four,” because there Abraham, Isaac and Jacob were laid, and Adam the first, as is plainly shown in the book of Josue.
03_marg701: Abraham rose up, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is asked how Abraham bowed down to the people of the land, when it is written: “The Lord thy God shalt thou adore, and him only shalt thou serve.” But it is not said in the commandment, “The Lord thy God only shalt thou adore,” as it is said, “and him only shalt thou serve.” For such service is owed to God alone as is called in Greek latreia. Whence idolaters are condemned, who show this service to idols. Nor should it trouble us that elsewhere an angel forbids a man to adore him and warns him that God rather should be adored. For he had appeared such that he could be adored in God’s place, and therefore the adorer had to be corrected.
03_marg702: JEROME. In the Hebrew, as we have set it down, the name is first written Ephron, and the second time Ephran. For after he was won over by the price to sell the sepulchre and take the silver, even though Abraham pressed him, the letter vau, which among them is read as o, was taken from his name, and instead of Ephron he was called Ephran. In which it is signified that he was not of perfect virtue who could sell the memorials of the dead. So let those know, who take the price of sepulchres not from those who press them but from the unwilling, that their name is changed and something of their merit perishes, since even he is blamed who took it unwillingly.

03_marg703: And the field … was made sure, etc. GREGORY. Morally. The double sepulchre hints that the perfect preacher hides the soul that has died to the desires of the flesh under the covering of good work and of contemplation, so that it may lie hidden from fleshly concupiscence as if without feeling; which before, feeling it, lived mortally. Whence: “For you are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.” For the active life buries the dead from wicked works; the contemplative more perfectly, since it divides them utterly from all actions. So he who has already tamed in himself the insults of the flesh has still to exercise his mind in the pursuits of holy work; and he who already enlarges his mind through holy works has still to stretch it to the secrets of inmost contemplation. For he is not a perfect preacher who, for the pursuit of contemplation, neglects what is to be done, or, for the urgency of work, puts off what is to be contemplated.
03_marg704: The double cave, etc. And the wooded field around it is bought by the patriarch from the lords of the land for four hundred sicles of silver, to bury Sara; because for preachers to have leisure for wisdom and to give themselves to action, under the leaves of mystical words as under fruitful trees, a quiet place is not otherwise gained than if, by the gospel teaching shining with the brightness of silver, eternal happiness is urged by them upon the earthly powers. Which is well figured by a hundred multiplied by four, which is moved from the left hand to the right.

03_marg711: Now, therefore, the maid to whom I shall say, etc. AUGUSTINE. It is to be asked how unlawful auguries differ from this petition, by which the servant asks that God show him the one who was to be Isaac’s wife, by whom, when he asked to drink, it should be said: “Drink, and I will give thy camels drink also.” But it is one thing to ask for something that is a sign by its very wonder; another to watch things which happen in such a way that they are not wonderful, but are interpreted by diviners with superstitious vanity. But even this very thing, that some wonder is asked for by which what one wishes to know is signified, whether it should be heard, is no small question. For it belongs to what those are said to do who do this wrongly: to tempt God. Whence: “Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God.” For it was suggested to Christ, as to a man, that he should find out by some sign how much he could do with God; which is done wrongly. From this is distinguished what Gedeon did when the danger of battle hung over him; for that was a consulting of God rather than a tempting. Whence Achaz fears to ask a sign, lest he seem to tempt God, when the Lord warned him here through the prophet; perhaps thinking that he was being tested by the prophet whether he remembered the command by which tempting God is forbidden.

03_marg713: GREGORY. Allegorically. Every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer; therefore the servant asks, Rebecca gives drink, because the Church of the elect satisfies the desire of the preachers by the strength of her faith. For she who confesses the God whom she hears offers the preacher the water of refreshment and coolness. And it is to be noted that she lowered the pitcher from her shoulder, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from good work. Or she gave water because in what she believed she did not remain empty; for she soon preached what she heard, and by teaching brought forth many preachers from herself. For the water in the pitcher is the knowledge of preaching in measure; for she strives “not to be more wise than it behoveth to be wise.” The pitcher on the arm is the measure of preaching in work. And she gives drink not only to all his companions but to the camels too, because the word of life is preached not only to the prudent but to fools as well. Whence: “To the wise and to the unwise I am a debtor.” Or water is given to the beasts too, when it is set in order how the care of the flesh is to be had, so that it is not spent on pleasure nor denied to need. Whence: “Make not provision for the flesh in its concupiscences.” And elsewhere: “No man ever hated his own flesh.”

03_marg721: And my master made me swear, etc. AUGUSTINE. The sense is the same; not all the words were said, either the same ones or in that way; which must be said because of those who slander the evangelists, that in some words they do not altogether agree, when the things and the senses are the same. For one man wrote this book, who could have set down what he said above, when Abraham gave his charge, or the rest, if he judged it to belong to the matter; since the truth of a narrative requires only that there be truth of the things and the senses, by which the will (to make which known words are made) appears sufficiently.
03_marg722: JEROME. In the Hebrew it is written: “Behold I stand by the well of water, and it shall be that the young maiden who comes out to draw,” etc. For “young maiden” in the Hebrew is read alma, as in Isaias, where in our books it is written, “Behold a virgin shall conceive,” etc.; in the Hebrew is read, “Behold an alma shall conceive.” So it is to be noted that alma always signifies a virgin and has the etymology apocrypha, that is, “hidden.” For in Job, where it is written of wisdom, “and it is hid from the eyes of all living,” in the Hebrew it is said naalma. So alma, which is interpreted “hidden,” that is, a virgin guarded with very great care, seems to be of greater praise than virgo. For one can be a virgin in body and not in spirit or mind; but she who is hidden has an addition to virginity, so that she is both a virgin and hidden; and she who is hidden, according to the idiom of the Hebrew tongue, is consequently a virgin too; but she who is a virgin is not at once hidden. This same word we read in Exodus of Mary, Moses’ sister, still a virgin. So let the Jews show anywhere alma put where it sounds “young maiden” and not “virgin.”

03_marg724: And bringing forth vessels of silver, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. After the servant had won the cause of the marriage, he gave all these to Rebecca; because the teachers of the Church give her as many ornaments as the good virtues they have taught. For she who had first received earrings and bracelets now receives vessels of gold and silver and garments; because the Church, which before received faith, obedience and working, growing, grows strong in spiritual things, so that, filled with the spirit of prophecy and the grace of virtues, she grows with enlarged gifts. Gifts are offered to the mother and brother, because the Gentile world, from the time the Church came to the faith, has grown strong in temporal glory. For everywhere Christians feel affliction, Gentiles glory in earthly strength. Her brothers receive gifts; for those who in the Church hold the faith in word, but yet do not follow their profession in manners, are honoured by the faithful because they are called faithful. So the mother and brothers receive gifts, but are strangers to the inheritance; because the unbelieving or the fleshly do not come to the eternal inheritance, but obtain the glory of the bounty above in temporal things.

03_marg729: At the same time, etc. GREGORY. Allegorically. The Living and the Seeing is the Lord, of whom it is written: “I live for ever, saith the Lord.” And elsewhere: “All things are naked and open to his eyes.” The well is the depth of holy Scripture, which waters our minds. The way is the humility of Christ’s passion, through which the streams of Scripture have been opened to us. For unless Christ, incarnate, had been tempted, seized, buffeted, spat upon, crucified and dead, the depth of Scripture would not lie open. So the humility of the passion became the key of the opening, so that we may drink the water of knowledge from the deep. For we understand these things, heard before, now done, which were read before and not understood. Whence: “The lion of the tribe of Juda hath prevailed to open the book and to loose the seals thereof.” But it is to be noted that he does not say “walked” but “walked about.” For he walks about who treads a way by going and returning. In the humility of the passion Christ walked about, because he bore now insults of words, now false witness, now blows, now spittle, now a crown of thorns, now the cross.

In the Hebrew is read: “Isaac went forth to speak in the field, the evening now declining”; where it is signified that the Lord prayed alone on the mountain; and that Isaac, who was a type of the Lord, as a just man gone out of his house for prayer at the ninth hour or before sunset, offered spiritual victims to God.
03_marg732: The field is the world, into which Christ went forth, because he deigned to appear visible. Whence: “Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people.” Isaac goes out to meditate in the field, because Christ, giving the form of humility, showed the exercise of long-suffering and the examples of passion and patience, as young men practised in the use of arms are wont to drill. The drill of arms is the frequent bearing of the passion. For he who bore blows, spittle, the lance and the cross allowed the passion even to death to be often borne in himself. We call sufferings arms, because through them we are freed from the adversary. Whence: “In your patience you shall possess your souls.”

03_marg734: Lighted off the camel, etc. GREGORY. Rebecca is brought to Isaac on a camel, because Rebecca signifies the Church, the camel the Gentile people, twisted in manners and loaded with the worship of idols. For those who found for themselves, out of themselves, gods to worship, had a burden grow on their back from them, to carry. So the Church, hastening to Christ from the Gentile world, is found in the twisted ways of the old life. On seeing Isaac she gets down from the camel, because, recognising her Redeemer more closely, she humbly forsakes the pursuits of the fleshly life, and herself speaks against her own twistedness, and seeks humility from the height of pride. Sitting on the camel she saw Isaac, because, still leaning on vices, she went up clinging not yet to spiritual but to animal manners. 03_marg762: Esau swore to him, etc. GREGORY. It is to be known that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it forestalls the time of need. Sometimes it does not forestall the time, but seeks daintier foods. Sometimes it desires that what is to be taken be prepared more carefully. Sometimes it suits the kind of food and the time, but goes beyond measure in the quantity taken. And sometimes what it desires is base, and yet it sins worse by the very heat of the desire. Jonathan earned the sentence of death because in tasting the honey he forestalled the appointed time of eating. The people led out of Egypt fell in the desert because, despising the manna, they asked for flesh, which they thought daintier. The first fault of the sons of Heli is that, at their wish, the priest’s servant would not receive the meat of the sacrifice boiled, as was the custom, but sought it raw, to serve it up more carefully. And when it is said, “This was the iniquity of Sodom, pride, fulness of bread and abundance,” it is shown that it perished because, with the vice of pride, it went beyond the measure of refreshment. Hence Esau lost his birthright, because he desired with great heat a contemptible food, that is, lentils; and the vice is not in the food but in the appetite. Whence we often take daintier foods without fault, and taste baser ones with the guilt of concupiscence. For Esau lost the first place for lentils; Elias in the desert kept his strength by eating flesh. Hence the devil, because he understands that not food but concupiscence is the cause of damnation, subdued the first man to himself not by flesh but by an apple, and tempted the second by bread. Hence it is that the fault of Adam is often committed even when cheap things are taken. For Adam was not the only one to receive a prohibition to abstain from the apple. For when God points out foods contrary to our health, he forbids them to us as by a sentence; and when, desiring harmful things, we touch them, we taste what is forbidden. But those things are to be taken which the need of nature asks, and not those which the lust of eating suggests.

It is asked when this was done, that Isaac went to Gerara: whether after Esau sold his birthright, for these things are told in a row; or whether, as is often done, the narrator went back to them by summing-up, when, having gone on about his sons, he had come to the place where the lentils are recalled. For the Abimelech is found who had also desired Sara; for his groomsman and the captain of his army, who were recalled there, are recalled here too. But it raises the question whether they could have been alive. For when he became Abraham’s friend, Isaac was not yet born, but promised. Let us suppose that that was done before Isaac was born; then Isaac received his sons when he was sixty years old. And they were young men when Esau sold his birthright; let us suppose them to have been about twenty, and Isaac’s years up to that deed of his sons come to about eighty. Let us take Abimelech too to have been a young man when he desired his mother and became Abraham’s friend; so he could have been about a hundred, if Isaac went to Gerara after that deed of his sons. So from this no necessity compels us to think that Isaac’s journey is told by summing-up. But because it is written there that he was there long, dug wells, contended over them, and grew rich in wealth, it is no wonder if it is said by summing-up, having been passed over so that the account of the sons might first come down to the lentils. And so what is written of Isaac, “God blessed him, and the man was exalted,” etc., is said according to earthly happiness, as what follows teaches. So although these things signify something spiritual, yet as to the way in which they happened, “God blessed him” is put first, so that we may understand that temporal things can neither be given nor should prosper except from the one God.

03_marg774: To which place, etc. JEROME. Abimelech does not always have peace with Isaac. Sometimes he is at odds, sometimes he seeks peace. And he signifies the studious and wise of the world, who through the learning of philosophy have grasped much of the truth. He is neither always in dissension with Isaac (who signifies the word of God) nor always in peace. For philosophy is neither contrary to the divine law in everything nor in harmony with it in everything. For many of the philosophers write that there is one God who created all things. And some have even added that he made and rules all things through his Word, and that it is the Word of God by which all things are governed; in which they agree with the Gospel too. And moral and natural philosophy hold almost all that is ours; but they differ when they say that matter is coeternal with God, and deny that God cares for mortal things, saying that his providence is confined above the space of the lunar sphere; and that he lays out the lives of those born by the courses of the stars; and when they say that the world is perpetual and to be closed by no end. 03_marg775: For Ochozath the groomsman, in the Hebrew there is “the company of his friends,” so that it signifies as much a man as the crowd of friends who had come with the king, among whom was Phicol the captain of his army.
03_marg776: ISIDORE. Two came with Abimelech: Ochozath his son-in-law, and Phicol the captain of the army. Ochozath is interpreted “holding,” Phicol “the mouth of all,” Abimelech “my father the king.” These three hold the image of the whole of philosophy, which is divided into three parts: logic, physics, ethics, that is, the rational, the natural, the moral. The rational is that which confesses God as Father of all, as Abimelech is. The natural is that which is fixed and holds all things, as if resting on the powers of nature itself, which Ochozath, who is called “holding,” professes. The moral is that which is in the mouth of all, belongs to all, and, because of the likeness of common precepts, is turned over in the mouths of all; which Phicol signifies, who is interpreted “the mouth of all.” So all these, instructed in these learnings, come to the law of God, saying: “We saw that the Lord is with thee,” etc. They ask for a blessing, not a repayment. Whence follows: “So he made them a feast”; for he who ministers the word is a debtor to the wise and to the unwise.
03_marg777: And behold the same day, etc. JEROME. I do not know how in the Seventy it is had: “And the servants of Isaac came, telling him of the well which they had dug, and they said to him: We have not found water; and he called its name Oath.” For what etymology is there in its being called Oath because they did not find water? And on the contrary in the Hebrew, with which rendering Aquila and Symmachus agree, it signifies that they found water, and that therefore the well itself was called “Fullness,” and the city Bersabee, that is, “the well of fullness.” For though above we asserted that Bersabee was named from the word of swearing, or from the number seven of the sheep, which is called sabee, yet now, from the finding of water, Isaac, alluding to the name of the city, bent the letter a little, and for the hissing shin of the Hebrews, with which sabee begins, put the Greek sigma, that is, the Hebrew samech. And according to the allegory too, after so many wells, at the end of the virtues, it does not fit that Isaac should not find water.
